title: Q2’s resilience doesn’t mean European consumer spending is set to take off
gist: Oxford Economics (Duncan Campbell) argues eurozone consumer spending's 0.4% q/q Q2 2026 gain was flattered by one-offs (fiscal support, an EV purchase surge, a falling savings rate) and expects an H2 slowdown driven mainly by food and energy inflation squeezing real incomes rather than by interest rates, though a consumer recession is seen as unlikely.

insights.claim: European (eurozone) consumer spending grew 0.4% q/q in Q2 2026, a surprisingly resilient outturn.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Headline Q2 consumption beat should not be extrapolated into H2 growth forecasts.
insights.quote: growing by 0.4% quarter-on-quarter, but this strength may be overstated

insights.claim: Q2 eurozone consumption was flattered by one-off factors: fiscal support for lower-income households and a surge in electric vehicle purchases.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Non-recurring boosts imply payback risk; EV/autos demand pull-forward may fade in H2.
insights.quote: One-off factors, such as fiscal support for lower-income households and a surge in electric vehicle purchases

insights.claim: A fall in the household savings rate helped lift Q2 spending, but further declines are unlikely given elevated uncertainty and high interest rates.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The savings drawdown tailwind is exhausted; consumption must rely on real income growth.
insights.quote: this is unlikely to continue in the coming quarters due to elevated uncertainty and interest rates

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects European consumer spending growth to slow in H2 2026, driven by inflation and a lower contribution from household savings.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Underweight eurozone consumer-discretionary exposure relative to consensus extrapolating Q2.
insights.quote: A slowdown is anticipated in H2, driven by inflation and a decline in household savings

insights.claim: The coming consumer slowdown is primarily a real-income story (food and energy inflation eroding purchasing power) rather than an interest-rate story.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: ECB rate cuts would do little to revive spending; energy/food price path is the key variable to watch.
insights.quote: primarily linked to real income challenges rather than interest rates

insights.claim: Despite the expected slowdown, the risk of an outright eurozone consumer recession remains low.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Downside is a soft patch, not a collapse; avoid pricing a consumption recession.
insights.quote: the risk of a consumer recession remains low

insights.claim: Lower-income households' spending has held up surprisingly well despite rising staples prices, partly thanks to fiscal support.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Resilience at the bottom of the income distribution is policy-dependent and vulnerable if support is withdrawn.
insights.quote: lower-income households’ spending has held up surprisingly well

insights.claim: Softening hospitality spending suggests consumers are making precautionary cutbacks.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Hospitality and discretionary services are an early-warning indicator of the H2 slowdown.
insights.quote: spending on hospitality services has softened, indicating potential precautionary cutbacks
